reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes Baked Beans 2.0 by promising 3% daily returns and up to 6% through link sharing while directing viewers to connect a wallet, hold BNB, and buy into the project. It describes referral-based earnings and a mechanism in which new money pays earlier participants, with additional investment required to continue receiving profit. Despite an invest-at-your-own-risk disclaimer, the presentation remains a favorable solicitation to fund and participate in the project.

opening.argument: The presentation expressly discloses uncertainty and personal risk rather than disguising the nature of the opportunity. The speaker says, “I am NOT a financial advisor” and calls the discussion “not financial advice,” while directing viewers to invest only what they are willing to lose. The description repeats the same warning. That framing matters: viewers are told to evaluate the opportunity at their own risk, not promised protection or guaranteed success. The stated return and project mechanics are presented as disclosed terms, accompanied by an explicit warning that participation can result in loss.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing argument treats the discussion of “3% daily” as a promise, but the same presentation identifies the speaker as not a financial advisor and tells viewers to accept the risk themselves. The quoted lock condition describes a project rule, not evidence that the creator concealed the possibility of loss. The existence of a favorable description does not erase the prominent warning that viewers should invest only what they are willing to lose.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A disclaimer does not neutralize the video's substantive solicitation. The speaker calls the project “awesome,” says viewers can earn daily returns, and explicitly acknowledges that new money pays old money. Warning viewers about risk while encouraging them to participate still leaves the central promotional message intact; it does not make the return representation merely neutral commentary.

opening.argument: The video's observable format is an operational walkthrough of how the platform works. It explains connecting a wallet, using the interface, compounding or “rebaking,” the timing rules, fees, and the maximum payout, then reports the speaker's own account status. This is instructional and demonstrative content: viewers are shown the process and the stated mechanics so they can understand what the interface does. Explaining how a tool operates, including its limitations and costs, is not by itself proof that the creator is certifying the tool or guaranteeing an outcome.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing side infers solicitation from a walkthrough and a link, but demonstrating a platform necessarily involves showing how to connect and operate it. The speaker also explains fees, timing, and limits rather than concealing them. A personal walkthrough can be educational even when the presenter expresses an opinion about the project; the cited mechanics do not establish that viewers were guaranteed a result.

opening.argument: The material can be understood as a disclosed referral-based promotion for a digital platform, not proof of a deceptive scam mechanism. The displayed interface presents a “Buy Beans” control, while the referral documentation lays out tiered bonuses and a minimum deposit condition. Those are visible program terms, and the supplied material does not show credential collection, a completed payout, or an independently verified loss. Referral rewards and promotional links can exist in ordinary platform marketing without establishing that the creator misrepresented safety or outcomes. The description also expressly identifies the activity as high risk and tells viewers to invest only what they are willing to lose.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opposing argument labels the presence of a purchase control and referral terms as the scam mechanism itself. But the supplied frames show disclosed interface elements and documentation, while the video expressly describes the arrangement as high risk. Referral bonuses and a promotional link do not, without more, establish credential theft, fabricated transactions, or a concealed outcome. The cited return language may describe the platform's stated terms, but it does not prove those terms were secretly misrepresented.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The disclosed interface does not make the arrangement ordinary commerce: it asks users to deposit BNB into a locked rewards pool while presenting recurring returns. The speaker also directs viewers to use a referral link and admits that new money pays earlier participants. Those facts describe an investment-pool and recruitment structure, not a conventional purchase of goods or services; lack of shown credentials or a completed payout is immaterial to the promotional claim.
